title: Electrical Circuits & Measurement — 50 MCQs
description: 50 MCQs on Kirchhoff's laws, Wheatstone & meter bridge, potentiometer, galvanometer conversions, superconductors and related measurements. Options are shuffled each load.

questions.q: Kirchhoff's current law (KCL) states:
options: Sum of currents entering a junction equals sum leaving
Sum of voltages around a loop equals zero
questions.explanation: KCL is conservation of charge at a junction: algebraic sum of currents = 0.

questions.q: Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL) is based on:
options: Conservation of energy around a closed loop
questions.explanation: KVL states algebraic sum of potential differences around any closed loop is zero.

questions.q: To find unknown currents in a multi-loop circuit one typically:
options: Apply KCL and KVL to independent nodes/loops and solve simultaneous equations
Use only Ohm's law at one resistor
questions.explanation: Combine KCL and KVL with Ohm's law to form equations and solve for unknowns.

questions.q: In a Wheatstone bridge, balance condition is when:
options: No current flows through the galvanometer across the bridge
questions.explanation: Balance yields zero galvanometer current and relation R1/R2 = R3/R4.

questions.q: Wheatstone bridge balance condition in terms of resistances R1,R2,R3,Rx is:
questions.explanation: Balance occurs when ratio of two known arms equals ratio of other two arms; useful to find unknown Rx.

questions.q: A meter bridge is essentially a practical form of:
options: Wheatstone bridge using a uniform wire
questions.explanation: Meter bridge uses uniform wire as the bridge arm to compare resistances using null deflection.

questions.q: In the meter bridge balance method, the null point is located by:
options: Moving jockey until galvanometer shows zero current
questions.explanation: Null deflection indicates balanced lengths and allows calculation of unknown resistance by length ratios.

questions.q: A potentiometer is used primarily to:
options: Measure emf and compare emfs without drawing current from the source
questions.explanation: Potentiometer provides a null method to measure emf and internal resistance without loading the source.

questions.q: Working principle of potentiometer is based on:
options: Uniform potential gradient along a wire carrying constant current
questions.explanation: A constant current through a uniform wire produces a linear potential drop; lengths correspond to emfs.

questions.q: To convert a galvanometer into an ammeter you should:
options: Connect a low-value shunt resistor in parallel with the galvanometer
Connect a high resistance in series
questions.explanation: A shunt bypasses most current so only a fraction passes through galvanometer; appropriate shunt calibrates range.

questions.q: To convert a galvanometer into a voltmeter you should:
options: Connect a high resistance in series with the galvanometer
questions.explanation: Series resistance limits current for a given voltage, allowing measurement over a larger voltage range.

questions.q: A perfect conductor (ideal conductor) differs from a superconductor because:
options: Perfect conductor has zero resistance but does not necessarily expel magnetic field; superconductor exhibits Meissner effect
Both are identical in all properties
Perfect conductors operate at low temperature only
questions.explanation: Superconductors show zero resistance and expel magnetic fields (Meissner); an ideal perfect conductor conceptually has zero resistivity but lacks Meissner behavior.

questions.q: Superconductivity is characterized by:
options: Zero electrical resistance below critical temperature and expulsion of magnetic field (Meissner effect)
questions.explanation: Superconductors have zero resistance and exhibit Meissner effect below a critical temperature.

questions.q: Critical temperature of a superconductor is:
options: Highest temperature the material can reach
Temperature at which resistance is maximum
questions.explanation: Superconductors transition to zero resistance at temperatures below their critical temperature (Tc).

questions.q: In a balanced potentiometer measurement to compare two emfs, null point ensures:
options: No current flows through the galvanometer so emf comparison is unaffected by current draw
questions.explanation: Null method avoids drawing current from test cell, giving accurate emf comparison.

questions.q: Potentiometer is preferred over a voltmeter for accurate emf measurement because:
options: It is a null method and does not load the source
questions.explanation: Null measurement avoids internal resistance effects and yields precise emf without drawing current from source.

questions.q: Internal resistance of a cell can be measured using potentiometer by:
options: Comparing the terminal emf under load and open-circuit emf using length ratios
Using a voltmeter placed across a short
questions.explanation: Potentiometer can determine lost voltage under load and hence internal resistance by comparing emfs.

questions.q: Wheatstone bridge is most accurate for measuring:
options: Resistances of moderate value with high precision
Very low resistances below milliohm only
questions.explanation: Wheatstone bridge gives precise resistance ratio measurements when bridge arms are chosen suitably.

questions.q: In practical Wheatstone bridge the galvanometer least sensitive at balance; best accuracy comes when:
options: Galvanometer is sensitive and null is sharp
questions.explanation: High sensitivity galvanometer allows detecting small imbalances leading to precise determination of balance point.

questions.q: In meter bridge experiment the ratio of resistances is equal to:
options: Ratio of lengths on the wire (l1/l2) at null point
Ratio of areas of wire segments
questions.explanation: At balance, unknown/known resistance = corresponding length ratio on uniform wire.

questions.q: If a galvanometer has resistance G and full-scale current Ig, to convert it into a voltmeter of range V, series resistance R should be:
questions.explanation: Total resistance required = V/Ig; subtract galvanometer resistance to get series resistor.

questions.q: To convert a galvanometer to an ammeter for range I, required shunt Rs is:
questions.explanation: Shunt divides current: Ig through galvanometer and remainder through shunt. Rs derived from current division.

questions.q: A potentiometer wire of length L carries a constant current. The potential gradient is uniform because:
options: Wire is uniform and current is constant so drop per unit length is constant
questions.explanation: Uniform wire and constant current produce linear potential drop; used for measurements.

questions.q: While measuring internal resistance of a cell with potentiometer, the terminal emf under load is measured by connecting:
options: A known external resistance across the cell and noting new null length
questions.explanation: Comparing emf under load to open-circuit emf gives voltage drop due to internal resistance; known external resistor allows calculation.

questions.q: Superconductors are used in practical devices such as:
questions.explanation: Large superconducting magnets and SQUIDs exploit zero resistance and strong fields for applications.

questions.q: Type I and Type II superconductors differ by:
options: Their behavior in magnetic fields — Type II allows mixed state with vortices at higher fields
questions.explanation: Type II have two critical fields and a vortex mixed state; Type I show abrupt transition and complete Meissner behavior below critical field.

questions.q: Meissner effect refers to:
options: Complete expulsion of magnetic field from a superconductor below critical temperature
questions.explanation: Meissner effect distinguishes superconductors from perfect conductors: magnetic flux is expelled when cooling into superconducting state.

questions.q: A potentiometer compares two emfs directly by adjusting length such that:
options: Potential drop along wire equals emf of test cell at null
questions.explanation: Null ensures potential difference between tapping point and reference equals emf under test.

questions.q: In potentiometer method, source current must be kept constant because:
options: Potential gradient along wire must remain constant for accurate comparison
questions.explanation: Stable current ensures linear potential gradient; fluctuations would change null lengths and introduce error.

questions.q: A practical difficulty in converting galvanometer to voltmeter is ensuring:
options: Series resistance is high enough to limit current but not so high to affect accuracy
Internal resistance of battery is zero
questions.explanation: Series resistor must be chosen to provide desired range while keeping meter sensitivity and loading acceptable.

questions.q: Wheatstone bridge sensitivity increases when bridge arms are chosen so that:
options: Balance point occurs near mid-scale of galvanometer sensitivity
questions.explanation: Choosing arms so balance is near mid-range yields maximum sensitivity for small changes.

questions.q: In meter bridge if lengths measured at null are l1 and l2 then unknown resistance Rx relates to known R as:
questions.explanation: At balance Rx/R = l1/l2 where l1 is length corresponding to Rx side.

questions.q: If galvanometer coil has large resistance, converting to ammeter requires:
options: A very small shunt to pass most current
questions.explanation: High coil resistance means most current must bypass through low-value shunt to measure larger currents.

questions.q: Sensitivity of potentiometer measurement improves with:
options: Longer potentiometer wire and stable low-drop source current
questions.explanation: Longer wire gives larger measurable length per emf; stable current reduces drift.

questions.q: Galvanometer ideal characteristic for precise null detection is:
options: High sensitivity (deflection per unit current) and low zero offset
questions.explanation: High sensitivity enables detecting very small currents for accurate null detection.

questions.q: When using potentiometer to measure internal resistance of a cell, internal resistance r is obtained from known external resistance R and measured emfs E_open and E_loaded by:
questions.explanation: From voltage division: terminal voltage E_loaded = E_open * (R/(R + r)); solving yields r = R*(E_open - E_loaded)/E_loaded.

questions.q: A superconductor cooled below Tc carries a persistent current because:
options: There is zero resistance so current persists without applied voltage
Current is blocked by Meissner effect
questions.explanation: Zero resistivity allows persistent currents to circulate indefinitely in closed superconducting loops.

questions.q: Distinction between perfect conductor and superconductor: perfect conductor hypothetical behavior does not include:
options: Meissner effect (flux expulsion) which superconductors exhibit
questions.explanation: Perfect conductor concept lacks Meissner effect; superconductors show flux exclusion, a distinct thermodynamic property.

questions.q: A Kelvin bridge is used to measure:
options: Low resistances accurately by eliminating lead and contact resistance
questions.explanation: Kelvin (double bridge) measures small resistances accounting for lead resistances via four-terminal connections.

questions.q: In practical potentiometer an auxiliary battery is used to:
options: Provide current for potentiometer wire independent of test cell
questions.explanation: Auxiliary battery supplies current through potentiometer wire producing required potential gradient across wire.

questions.q: Null deflection methods are preferred because:
options: They minimize systematic loading errors and can be highly precise
They are faster than direct measurement always
questions.explanation: Null methods draw no current from test source at balance, eliminating loading errors and enabling high precision.

questions.q: An ammeter should ideally have:
options: Very low internal resistance to avoid altering circuit current
Very high resistance to avoid loading
questions.explanation: Low internal resistance minimizes voltage drop and disturbance to the circuit when measuring current.

questions.q: A voltmeter ideally should have:
options: Very high resistance so it draws negligible current
questions.explanation: High input resistance reduces loading effect on measured circuit element.

questions.q: When calibrating a voltmeter using potentiometer, main advantage is:
options: Avoiding direct current through meter during calibration (null method)
questions.explanation: Null comparison prevents loading of reference source, leading to accurate calibration.

questions.q: In Wheatstone bridge measurement the presence of contact resistance at nodes mainly affects accuracy when:
options: Contact resistances are comparable to measured resistances
questions.explanation: Large contact resistances disturb balance; four-terminal or Kelvin methods reduce this error.

questions.q: Practical meter bridge wire should be:
options: Uniform cross-section and material to ensure uniform resistance per unit length
questions.explanation: Uniform wire ensures linear potential gradient and valid length-to-resistance ratio assumptions.

questions.q: When converting galvanometer to voltmeter, the series resistor must be chosen knowing:
options: Galvanometer full-scale current and galvanometer resistance and desired voltage range
questions.explanation: Series R = V_range/Ig - Rg; need Ig and Rg to size R for desired range.

questions.q: A superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) is used to measure:
options: Extremely small magnetic flux changes with very high sensitivity
Large currents in power lines only
questions.explanation: SQUIDs exploit superconductivity and quantum interference to detect minute magnetic flux changes.

questions.q: To measure an unknown emf by potentiometer, first we determine the balancing length l0 for standard cell emf E0, then for test emf E1 balance length l1. The relation is:
questions.explanation: Potential gradient is constant, so emf ∝ balancing length; ratio gives emf comparison.

questions.q: Which statement about superconductors is correct regarding resistance below Tc?
options: Dc resistance is zero but AC may show losses (depending on frequency and material)
Resistance negligible only at high currents
Resistance is high at low temperatures
questions.explanation: Superconductors show zero DC resistance; AC losses can occur due to flux motion, hysteresis in Type II, or normal regions at high frequency.
